title: Locked Gates and Steerage Deaths: How White Star Priced Third-Class Passengers as Ballast
participants: International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Steerage fares collected from roughly 2,200 passengers, including masses of third-class emigrants, funded a luxury vessel whose lifeboat capacity was calculated for a fraction of those aboard — the skim was structural, priced into the ticket.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Passenger safety law of the era tied lifeboat requirements to tonnage rather than souls carried, allowing White Star to run a legally compliant vessel that could not evacuate its own manifest; physical barriers and gate arrangements between steerage and the boat deck compounded the deficit.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Third-class passengers, many of them immigrants with limited English, were left without guidance or accessible routes upward as the ship foundered; the ship's navigation at speed through a known ice field was normalized in company testimony as routine seamanship.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The transatlantic emigrant trade's dominant carriers captured fares on the promise of speed and grandeur while externalizing death risk onto the cheapest-fare class; Ismay's survival preserved the managing director who embodied that cost-transfer model.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Mersey inquiry focused its findings on crew conduct and seamanship rather than company policy, declined to censure Ismay, and closed the liability loop for the parent company; the US Smith Committee pressed harder but the British verdict became the operative record.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: White Star inherited the tonnage-based lifeboat regulatory regime and the transatlantic shipping cartel's immunity from soul-based capacity mandates, both established machinery of cost externalization.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1913-1914 SOLAS convention created the first binding international maritime safety framework, mandating lifeboat capacity for all aboard and institutionalizing state enforcement of carrier obligations.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Because SOLAS framed the remedy as equipment mandates and procedural rules rather than liability for the corporate gate-and-fare architecture, the carriers kept their fare structures and reputations; Ismay retired un-censured and the company escaped structural indictment.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The Mersey model — a state-commissioned inquiry that indicts operational staff while absolving corporate policy — became the template for later disaster tribunals across extraction industries, deferring liability indefinitely.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The iceberg-as-villain narrative, amplified by the legend of the doomed unsinkable ship, cast the sinking as an act of nature and bad luck rather than a costed business decision.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Icebergs do not lock steerage gates, under-stock lifeboats to tonnage rules, or run at speed through a reported ice field; the class-gradient death toll — proportionally far higher in third class than first — is the ledger entry the iceberg story erases.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Contemporary reports and the 1912-1913 US Senate Smith Committee inquiry documented locked gates and passageway arrangements hindering third-class access to the boat deck; the British Wreck Commissioner (Mersey) inquiry investigated the loss and has been criticized as a whitewash for its focus on crew conduct over company policy; the SOLAS convention followed.
